title: Chapter 102 – Heng's Favor
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The first frost comes down on the Inner Court like a held breath let out.

Jian wakes to it on the ninth morning of the ninth month, in the gray light of his cell, with the window furred white and his left arm gone cold to the bone. He lies still and listens. The mountain is silent. The streams that talked all summer have fallen quiet, and the pines on the ridge stand rimed and motionless against a sky the color of pewter. He pushes back his sleeve.

The green thread in the Spring Vein is still there, but it is a faint one now, thin as a hair, and when he lays his palm on the sill, where a few last blades of grass are stiffening in the cold, it does not answer. He holds it for the count of thirty. He tries again.

Dormant below freezing. The panel is quite clear on that.

"Three weeks," he says to Pebble. "Perhaps four. And it sleeps until the thaw."

Sleep, says Pebble from the pillow, with great feeling. All sleeps. Cold is rude.

He rolls the sleeve down. It is a bad loss, and it is also a known one. He has banked what he could: forty-five CE since the spring, kept in reserve like grain against a hard season. It will be the last he earns from the Vein for five months. After that, there will be only the Pill Hall at two points a night.

He is dressing when the knock comes. It is a boy from the Law Pavilion, breathless, with a folded paper in his fist.

"Deputy Rong's compliments, Gate Bearer. The prisoner Zhao Heng asks to see you. He says," the boy swallows, "that he is calling in a favor."

* * *

The cells of the Law Pavilion lie beneath the Pavilion itself, in a long low corridor of gray stone with an iron door at each end.

Deputy Rong meets him at the head of the stair. She is a broad quiet woman with a scar across her chin and the look of someone who has spent a great many nights awake. She says nothing at first. She leads him along the passage, past a row of locked doors, with the keys on her belt chinking softly at every step.

"He asked for you three days ago," she says, over her shoulder. "I put it off. I thought you should have your own mind." She stops at the last door. "He is worse."

"How much worse?"

"The Pill Hall gives him a year. Bai says six months, and does not say it to him." She fits a key to the lock. "The thread in his throat has spread. It is in the lung now. I have seen men die of the blood-thread before, and it is not quick."

"Does he know?"

"He has known since the day he confessed." She opens the door. "Go in. I will stand outside."

The cell is small and clean and cold. A cot, a stool, a table with a jug of water. A single barred window high in the wall, through which a stripe of pale light falls across the floor. On the cot, propped on a bolster with a gray blanket over his knees, sits a man who was once the finest swordsman in the Red Ridge.

Zhao Heng has shrunk.

It is the first thing Jian sees, and it shocks him more than he expects. The broad shoulders have fallen in. The heavy jaw has sharpened. The hair is white. His skin is the color of tallow, and across the base of the throat, just above the collar of the prison robe, a faint dark web creeps up from the chest like cracked glaze. He is breathing carefully, in short shallow draws, as a man breathes who has found out how much each one costs.

But the eyes are the same. Dark, steady, and a little amused.

"Gate Bearer," says Heng.

"Zhao Heng."

"You came."

"You called a favor."

"I did." The old man coughs. It is a wet, small sound. He lifts a hand, and the hand shakes. "Sit. There is only the stool. I apologize for the furniture."

Jian sits. For a moment neither of them speaks.

"They tell me you are a Foundation," says Heng. "At twenty-two."

"Early stage."

"At twenty-two." The ghost of a smile touches his mouth. "I was thirty-one when I reached it. I thought I was very fast." He wheezes. "I thought a great many things."

"You said you had a favor."

"Straight to the point. Good." Heng folds his hands on the blanket. "Let me say what it is, and what it will cost. And then you may refuse. I have no leverage. I have only a request."

* * *

"I have three things to ask," says Zhao Heng, "and one to give."

He speaks slowly, with long pauses. Jian listens without interrupting.

"The first thing to give is a key." He lifts his bound hand, and from beneath the bolster draws a small ring of black iron, with a thread of red cord knotted through it. "The thread-knot of the Red Ridge manor. It is the lock that holds my nephew Hui in the east wing. The steward, Pei, wears the matching knot on his wrist. As long as he lives, the boy is tied to him. If the steward dies, the boy dies. If this key is turned in the lock beside Hui's bed, the knot comes loose, and the steward's hold is broken, and he can do nothing." He lays it in Jian's palm. "It is warm. It is the family's oldest work. My grandfather made it."

Jian looks at the ring. It is warm. It hums, very faintly, under his thumb.

"Why give it to me?"

"Because I am dying, and there is no one else." Heng's voice is flat. "Qian is in custody. Bei is in the mines. Yao is fifteen and has broken with the family. The manor is held by a man I trusted, who has done a thing I cannot forgive." His mouth works. "I want the boy out. I should have wanted it a year ago. I wanted other things."

"And the second?"

"The second is a paper." A folded sheet, in his other hand. Jian takes it. It is a deed, in Heng's own square writing, with the Red Ridge seal beside the signature. I, Zhao Heng, Head of the Red Ridge Zhao, do convey the manor, lands, and holdings of the Red Ridge to the custody of the Outer Court, to be held in trust for the survivors of my family, under the supervision of the Gate Bearer. He reads it twice. "Deputy Rong has witnessed it. The Arbiter's clerk will seal it today."

"Under my supervision."

"Under the supervision of the only man in the Sect I think will not steal it." The dry amusement flickers. "Do not look at me like that, boy. I have spent forty years learning who steals. I know the shape of an honest man the way I know the shape of a sword."

Jian does not answer. He folds the deed and sets it on his knee.

"The third thing," says Heng, "is a request. It is not for me. It is for my family."

"Go on."

"When I die, I would like to be buried beside my niece." The voice drops. "Zhao Lin. Yao's sister. She is under the pines on the north slope of the Ridge, in a grave with no marker. I want to lie there. I want a stone with my name on it, and hers. I want Yao to put it up himself." He looks at the table. "I did not protect her. I did not protect any of them. It is the last thing I can ask of anyone."

The cell is silent. Outside, in the corridor, a key turns, and falls still.

"I will do it," Jian says.

"You have not heard the fourth."

"There is a fourth?"

"It is the one that costs." Heng's eyes come up. They are bright and very tired. "It is not for the family. It is for you. It is the favor."

* * *

"There is a letter," says Heng.

He draws it out from under the blanket, a single sheet, folded small and sealed with a drop of black wax. There is no mark on the outside but a name, in a clerk's neat hand.

Yan Zhi.

"I wrote it in the spring, after the trial. I have not been able to send it. Rong reads everything that leaves this cell, and I could not trust the carrier." He holds it between two fingers. "The man it is for lives at the Gray Peak way inn, a day's walk beyond the Sect's northern gate, in a house with a lamp over the door. He keeps an inn. He asks no questions. He was my friend, once, before I became what I became."

"A letter to an innkeeper."

"A letter to a man who used to work in an office." The old swordsman's gaze does not waver. "I want you to carry it. In person. Without the Sect's knowledge."

Jian goes very still.

"Without leave."

"Without leave."

"Why?"

"Because the Sect's gate-wardens report to the Registry." Heng's voice is almost soundless. "Every pass is copied. Every road is watched. The man in the lamp-house is the only person alive who can tell you what the Registry is, and what it wants, and what it did to my family. If you ask the Sect for a pass, they will know before you reach the gate. And he will be dead before you arrive."

The words fall in the cell like stones into a well.

"You know about the Registry," Jian says.

"I was its hand in the south for twenty years." Heng closes his eyes. "I am not proud of it. I am not telling you to make you think better of me. I am telling you because it is the only thing I have left that is worth something. I carried their orders. I paid their men. I bought their silence with my own family's blood." The thread at his throat pulses, faintly, black on tallow. "They have my nephew. They have had him for two years. They told me he would be safe if I was useful. I was very useful."

"And the Wellmaster?"

"An instrument. A knife. They sent him in to find the Gate." A shuddering breath. "They did not tell me he would use the Garden. I would have refused. I think I would have refused." He opens his eyes. "I am not certain. That is the worst of it."

Jian says nothing. He is aware of his own pulse, and the weight of the little ring in his palm, and the cold stripe of light on the floor.

"Take the letter," says Heng. "Please."

He takes it. The wax is still faintly warm.

"If I am caught outside the Sect without leave," he says, "the Law will strike my standing. Qin Hao's surety goes with it."

"Yes."

"You know that."

"I know it. I would not ask if there were another way." The old man lifts a hand, and lets it fall. "I am sorry. I have been sorry for a long time. It is of no use to anyone."

Jian looks at the letter. At the clerk's neat hand.

Yan Zhi.

He puts it inside his tunic.

* * *

Rong is waiting in the corridor when he comes out, leaning against the wall with her arms crossed.

She does not ask what was said. She has stood outside a hundred cell doors in her life, and she reads a closed face as other people read a letter. She pushes off the wall and walks beside him toward the stair, her boots loud on the stone.

"The deed," she says.

"I have it."

"I witnessed it. You will want to know that. I put my name under his, and my seal beside the Arbiter's, and I have told the clerk to file it in the third drawer, under Estates, Pending. It will sit there for a week before anyone looks. After that it is public." She stops at the foot of the stair. "I would not wait the week."

"No."

"Whatever it is you mean to do about the boy."

He looks at her. She meets it with her flat tired eyes.

"Deputy Rong."

"Gate Bearer."

"Why did you stand outside?"

She considers that, as though it were a harder question than he knew.

"Because I have been a deputy of Enforcement for twenty-six years," she says at last, "and in all that time I have never once been asked to find out who gives the orders. I have been asked to find who obeys. It is a different kind of work." Her voice is quiet. "In the winter you came to me with a thread-knot. I found eleven. I have not slept well since."

"You do not trust your own office."

"I trust Enforcement. I trust the men I trained. I do not trust the clerks who write our orders." She pulls her sleeve straight. "Someone above me has been reading my reports before I finish them. I have not found out who. I would very much like to."

"If I learn something, I will tell you."

"Do not tell me. Tell Ye. Ye tells me." A short grim twitch of her lips. "It is slower. It is safer."

She climbs the stair ahead of him, one hand on the rail, and he follows her up into the thin gray daylight with the deed against his chest and the little iron ring heavy in his palm.

* * *

Zhao Qian is in the next cell but one, and she asks for him by name.

Rong hesitates, and then unlocks the door. The room is the twin of Heng's: cold, clean, bare. A young woman sits on the cot with her back against the wall and her right arm held across her lap in a cloth sling. The wrist beneath the cloth is a ruin, a twisted knot of scar and bone, and the hand below it hangs curled and still. She is twenty-four. She looks forty. The Qian he remembers was proud and bright and quick with a blade. This one is quiet, with shadows under her eyes, and when he comes in she does not rise.

"Gate Bearer."

"Zhao Qian."

"I hear my uncle has called you."

"He has."

"I would have done it differently." The ghost of her old spirit shows in the set of her mouth. "But I have no right to an opinion. I was a fool in a house full of knives." She lifts her good hand. "I wanted to say two things. May I?"

"Please."

"The first is about the steward." Her eyes are steady. "Pei is a coward. He has Qi Refining peak and the courage of a rabbit. The thread-knot on his wrist is the only power he has, and he knows it. He drinks plum wine at dusk in the east gallery. He sleeps with his door barred and a lamp burning. He does not carry a blade because he cannot bear to be seen holding one." She pauses. "If you go at night, with the key, he will not stand against you. He will try to run."

"And Hui?"

"Hui is in the third room of the east wing. He has a cot and a window and a bowl of rice twice a day. He has not been beaten." Her voice cracks, very slightly. "He has not spoken in four months."

Jian says nothing.

"That is the second thing." She looks at the floor. "Tell him I am sorry. Tell him that his cousin Qian was a coward and a liar and that she loved him. Tell him it is not his fault." She draws a breath. "I do not expect him to forgive me. I only want him to know he was not the reason."

"I will tell him."

"Thank you." She lets her head rest against the wall. "I used to think the Zhao name was a thing to be proud of. I am learning what it costs. It is a very slow lesson."

He bows to her, a small correct bow, the sort one gives to an elder. She watches him go with something in her face he cannot name.

* * *

He tells only two people.

He tells Ye first, in the herbal room, with the door barred. She listens to the whole of it without a word, her pale eyes on the lamp, her hands folded on the scroll in her lap. When he is done she is silent for some time.

"I cannot give you a pass," she says.

"I know."

"The clerks who copy passes are mine. I trained them. I cannot say which of them reports to the Registry, and I will not find out by testing." Her voice is steady. "If you leave by the gate, they will know within the hour. If you leave without a pass, the Law will know within the day." She lifts her eyes. "Qin Hao must be told."

"Qin Hao will have to answer for it."

"Qin Hao has been answering for you since the winter." She rises and goes to the shelf, and takes down a small lacquer box, and opens it. Inside lies a thin brass key. "The Sutra Hall has a back stair. It descends from the lower vault to a postern in the north wall. It has not been used in a hundred years. The door is hidden by a rockfall. I found it by accident, in my third year as Elder."

"Elder—"

"I did not give you this." She lays the key in his palm. "I did not tell you where the stair is. I will say, if asked, that you were in the herbal room for the whole of the night." Her eyes are very clear. "I am forty years too old to be afraid of the Rule."

He closes his hand.

He tells Qin Hao second, at the fortieth landing, at dusk. The scholar-Guard sits on his stool with his blanket across his knees, listening, with his paper lantern at his elbow. He does not look up from his book. When Jian has finished, he turns a page.

"I did not hear that," says Qin Hao.

"No, Elder."

"I heard a young man ask for the date of the winter solstice." He turns another page. "It falls on the twenty-first day of the eleventh month. I will not be at my post on the night of the fourteenth of the tenth. I shall be in my bed, with a cold."

"Elder, I—"

"I said it was a cold." The old man's voice does not change. "Go and do whatever it is that you do not intend to tell me. And come back in one piece. I have a seat, a name, and sixty years in a bowl on the Arbiter's table. I would be grateful if you did not spend them."

"I will not."

"Hm." Qin Hao lifts his eyes. For a moment, in the lantern light, he looks every day of his age. "Lin Jian. I have told no one this. But I am very much afraid of what is coming. I think it is larger than any of us. I think you know that."

"I do."

"Then be careful." The scholar returns to his page. "Go."

* * *

Bai gives him a pill and an insult, in that order.

"Warm-heart," says the old Elder, tossing the lacquer box across the dispensary. "Two grains, a day. They keep the blood moving in the cold. They also keep the Qi from freezing in the channels, which is the thing that kills travelers on the northern road. You are a fool to go without them."

"I did not say I was going anywhere."

"You did not have to. You have been asking Zhong's boy about weather on the Gray Peak for three days." Bai peels a plum with his thumbnail. "I do not want to know. I do not want to be told. I am an old man who sells pills to anyone who asks, and I have been doing it for fifty years." He bites. "Take them."

Jian opens the box. Inside, packed in cotton, lie twelve small red pills, each the size of a bean.

"What is the cost?"

"Six hundred stones, at the Pill Hall's price. I will take it from your account as a deduction against the Garden dew." Bai chews. "It is not a favor. It is a bill. Do not mistake the two."

"I will not."

"Good." The old man looks at him. For a moment the small shrewd eyes lose their humor. "Lin Jian. You are very young to be carrying what you carry."

"I am twenty-two."

"I was twenty-two once. I thought I was very old." He turns back to the furnace. "Go. And come back. I have not finished teaching you to read a pulse."

Jian bows. He tucks the box inside his tunic, next to the letter.

The cost of a thing is also the shape of it, he thinks. And the shape of this one is a debt of six hundred stones to a man who says it is not a favor.

* * *

On the night before he leaves, Zhao Yao comes to his cell.

The boy has grown. He is fifteen now, tall and lean, with a burn scar over one brow and a way of standing very straight that he did not have a year ago. He wears the plain gray of an Outer disciple. He stops on the threshold with his hands at his sides.

"Brother Lin. They said my uncle has given you the key."

"He has."

"He has given you the deed too?"

"Yes."

Yao nods slowly. He looks at the floor, and then at the window, and then, with an effort, at Jian.

"I would like to go with you," he says. "To the manor. To get Hui."

"You cannot. I am going somewhere else first."

"Where?"

"I cannot say."

The boy's jaw tightens. "I have waited two years. I have been told 'later' by every Elder in the Sect. I have been told 'soon' by you." He swallows. "I do not say it to reproach. I say it because I do not know how much longer I can wait."

"Yao." Jian stands. "Listen to me. I will go to the manor. I will go in three weeks, perhaps four, when I come back. I will take you. You will be there when the door opens, and you will be the one to carry him out. I promise it."

"Three weeks."

"Four at most."

The boy takes a long breath. It trembles on the way out.

"There is something else," he says, very quietly. "I did not know whether to tell you. But my uncle called you for the favor, and he has given you the key, so I think you should know." He looks up. "My uncle was not the one who wrote the order for the Wellmaster."

Jian's skin prickles.

"Who wrote it?"

"I do not know. I found a copy, in the study at Red Ridge, when I was twelve. It was on plum-bark paper. There was no signature." His voice is hardly more than a breath. "But the seal at the bottom was not the Zhao seal. It was a small black square, with nothing in it."

Jian does not move.

The ones who wear no names.

Outside, a late wind has begun to rise. It rattles the frost on the shutters, and the lamp gutters, and for a moment the whole room is full of the sound of a mountain preparing for winter.

"Thank you, Yao," he says.

"Will it help?"

"It will help," says Jian. "It means that the man I am going to see may be telling the truth."
